exercises.title: Now your hand has to choose
exercises.body: Reading an ending is free — 𐑒𐑨𐑑𐑕 and 𐑛𐑪𐑜𐑟 simply say themselves. Writing one is where it bites, because English has trained your hand to reach for the same “-s” every time. It will want to. Say the word first, and let your throat answer instead: cats hisses, so 𐑕; dogs buzzes, so 𐑟.

exercises.title: The same trap, one letter later
exercises.body: Past tenses ambush you the same way. Your hand knows “-ed” and wants to type two letters for a sound that is only one: walked ends in a plain t, so 𐑢𐑷𐑒𐑑; played buzzes, so 𐑐𐑤𐑱𐑛. If you catch yourself about to write 𐑩𐑛 out of habit, stop and say the word.

exercises.title: When the beat is really there
exercises.body: 𐑩𐑛 is not the default — it is what you write only when the ending is a syllable you actually say, which happens after a t or d sound: 𐑢𐑪𐑯𐑑𐑩𐑛, 𐑯𐑰𐑛𐑩𐑛. Two beats or three? Count them on your fingers if you have to; the count decides, not the English spelling.

exercises.title: The easy one
exercises.body: After all that, -ing never changes: it is always 𐑦𐑙, the two letters you met together in Chapter 1. Running is 𐑮𐑳𐑯𐑦𐑙, singing is 𐑕𐑦𐑙𐑦𐑙 — with 𐑙 twice, because you say it twice.
